hook.text: In 2000, Pets.com sold dog food online, lost money on every sale, and was valued at $300 million. Then it was zero.

buildup.text: A bubble forms when asset prices far exceed intrinsic value, driven by speculation rather than fundamentals.

discovery.text: Economist Hyman Minsky identified three stages: displacement, euphoria, and panic. Every bubble follows this arc.

twist.text: Nobody knows they're in a bubble until it pops. During the ride, rising prices look like proof of value.

climax.text: Bubbles are recognized only in hindsight. That's what makes them dangerous and what makes them repeat.

punchline.text: If everyone sees it, it's not a bubble yet.

quiz.question: According to Minsky, what are the three stages of a bubble?

hook.text: You buy a stock at $100 knowing it's worth $50. You don't care—someone else will pay $120 tomorrow.

buildup.text: The greater fool theory: you can profit from an overpriced asset as long as a bigger fool buys it from you.

discovery.text: In a bubble, the price doesn't matter. What matters is momentum. Buyers don't calculate value; they chase returns.

twist.text: The last buyer is the greatest fool. When the music stops, whoever holds the asset absorbs the total loss.

climax.text: Every bubble participant thinks they'll sell before the crash. Statistically, most of them are wrong.

punchline.text: Everyone's a genius until the music stops.

quiz.question: What is the greater fool theory?
options: You can profit if someone else pays a higher price later

hook.text: In 2021, GameStop stock rose 1,500% in two weeks. Most buyers had never read a financial statement.

buildup.text: Herd behavior: people follow the crowd because everyone else can't be wrong. Social proof replaces analysis.

discovery.text: The mechanism is FOMO: fear of missing out. When your neighbor doubles their money, sitting out feels like losing.

twist.text: Herds amplify both buying and selling. The same crowd that pushes prices up causes stampede selling during crashes.

climax.text: Rational individuals become irrational groups. The psychology of crowds is the engine of every bubble.

punchline.text: Follow the crowd up. Follow them down.

quiz.question: What primarily drives herd behavior in financial markets?

hook.text: You have $10,000 and borrow $90,000 to invest. A 10% rise: 100% profit. A 10% fall: you're wiped out completely.

buildup.text: Leverage means borrowing to invest. It multiplies gains in good times and losses in bad times.

discovery.text: Cheap credit fuels bubbles. When loans are easy, speculation soars. Everyone borrows to buy more.

twist.text: When prices drop, leveraged investors get margin calls: pay up or we sell. Forced selling crashes prices further.

climax.text: Lehman Brothers was leveraged 30:1 in 2008. A 3% drop in assets wiped out all their capital.

punchline.text: Leverage turns a stumble into a cliff.

quiz.question: How does leverage amplify a financial bubble?
options: Borrowed money magnifies both gains and losses

hook.text: The NASDAQ lost 78% between 2000 and 2002. It took 15 years to recover. Some stocks never came back.

buildup.text: Bubbles pop when a trigger—bad news, a rate hike, a fraud exposed—shakes confidence. Selling begets selling.

discovery.text: The crash phase is faster than the bubble. It took years to build and weeks to collapse.

twist.text: The real damage isn't paper losses. It's bankruptcies, job losses, and a decade of reduced investment and trust.

climax.text: After every bubble, regulations tighten. After every recovery, they loosen. The cycle resets.

punchline.text: Build slowly. Break quickly. Repeat.

quiz.question: How long did it take the NASDAQ to recover from the 2000 crash?

hook.text: In 1637, a single tulip bulb sold for 10,000 guilders—enough to buy a canal house in Amsterdam.

buildup.text: Tulips arrived in Holland in the 1590s. Rare striped varieties became status symbols among the wealthy.

discovery.text: Speculators began trading tulip futures. People who'd never seen a tulip traded contracts on bulbs still in the ground.

twist.text: In February 1637, buyers stopped showing up at auction. Prices crashed 99% in days. Fortunes vanished overnight.

climax.text: Modern historians debate how widespread the mania was. But the story endures as the archetype of all bubbles.

punchline.text: A flower worth a fortune. Until it wasn't.

quiz.question: What made tulip mania the archetype of financial bubbles?
options: Tulips were the most expensive commodity
Prices skyrocketed on speculation then crashed 99%

hook.text: Isaac Newton lost $3.6 million in today's money in the South Sea Bubble. Even geniuses fall for bubbles.

buildup.text: In 1720, the South Sea Company took on Britain's national debt in exchange for trade monopoly rights.

discovery.text: The company had almost no actual trade. Its value was pure hype. Stock rose 800% in six months.

twist.text: Directors secretly sold their shares while promoting the stock. Insider trading before the term existed.

climax.text: The crash wiped out thousands and triggered the Bubble Act, banning joint-stock companies for over a century.

punchline.text: Newton said he could calculate the motions of stars but not the madness of men.

quiz.question: What was unusual about the South Sea Company?
options: It had almost no actual trade despite its huge valuation

hook.text: In the 1840s, Britain approved 9,500 miles of new railway. Only 6,220 miles were ever built. Investors lost billions.

buildup.text: Railways were transformative technology. Investors poured money into hundreds of competing railway companies.

discovery.text: Most routes were unprofitable. Too many companies served the same corridors, undercutting each other to death.

twist.text: The bubble bankrupted investors but left Britain with the world's best railway network. Destruction funded creation.

climax.text: The pattern repeats: transformative tech causes investment mania, a crash, then lasting infrastructure.

punchline.text: Wrong investors. Right technology. Great result.

quiz.question: What was the lasting result of railway mania?

hook.text: In 1720, shares in the Mississippi Company rose 2,000% in months. France's entire economy was a casino.

buildup.text: John Law convinced France to back paper money with shares in his Mississippi Company, which claimed vast riches.

discovery.text: Law created the world's first central bank-like system. Paper money replaced gold. Shares replaced bonds.

twist.text: The riches were imaginary. When investors demanded gold for their shares, there wasn't enough. Panic erupted.

climax.text: France's monetary system collapsed. The word 'bank' became taboo in French for decades.

punchline.text: One man built a financial system. It lasted two years.

quiz.question: What caused the Mississippi Bubble to collapse?
options: The claimed colonial riches were imaginary

hook.text: In 1989, the Imperial Palace in Tokyo was said to be worth more than all real estate in California combined.

buildup.text: Easy credit and speculation drove Japanese stocks and land to insane valuations throughout the 1980s.

discovery.text: The Nikkei peaked at 38,957 in December 1989. Companies like Nippon Telegraph were worth more than all U.S. stocks.

twist.text: When the Bank of Japan raised rates, the bubble popped. Stocks fell 80%. Real estate dropped 70%. Recovery took decades.

climax.text: Japan's lost decades prove bubbles don't just hurt investors. They can stall an entire nation for a generation.

punchline.text: The palace isn't overpriced anymore.

quiz.question: What triggered the collapse of Japan's asset bubble?
options: The Bank of Japan raised interest rates
A trade war with the U.S.

hook.text: Yahoo was worth more than the entire U.S. steel industry in 1999. It had 3,000 employees and no profits.

buildup.text: The internet was genuinely revolutionary. But investors treated every website like the next Microsoft.

discovery.text: Companies added '.com' to their names and stock prices doubled. Actual business models were optional.

twist.text: Amazon survived the crash, falling 93% before becoming a trillion-dollar company. Most others simply vanished.

climax.text: The dot-com bubble destroyed $5 trillion in market value. But the internet it funded changed everything.

punchline.text: The technology was real. The valuations weren't.

quiz.question: How much did Amazon's stock fall during the dot-com crash?

hook.text: The Dow Jones rose 500% between 1921 and 1929. Shoeshine boys gave stock tips. Then came Black Tuesday.

buildup.text: New technologies—radio, cars, electricity—created genuine wealth. But margin buying supercharged speculation.

discovery.text: Investors could buy $100 of stock with just $10 cash. The other $90 was borrowed. Leverage was everywhere.

twist.text: On October 29, 1929, the market lost 12% in one day. By 1932, stocks had fallen 89% from the peak.

climax.text: The crash triggered the Great Depression. Twenty-five percent unemployment. Bank failures nationwide.

punchline.text: The party ended. The hangover lasted a decade.

quiz.question: What amplified the stock market bubble of the 1920s?
options: Buying stocks on margin with borrowed money

hook.text: In 2021, 613 SPACs raised $162 billion. They were blank-check companies that bought things in the future, maybe.

buildup.text: SPACs let companies go public without the scrutiny of a traditional IPO. Celebrity sponsors added hype.

discovery.text: SPACs could make wild growth projections that regular IPOs couldn't. Future revenue estimates replaced actual earnings.

twist.text: By 2023, most SPAC stocks had lost 50-90% of their value. The sponsors kept their shares; investors took the losses.

climax.text: SPACs weren't innovation—they bypassed rules meant to protect investors. Deregulation disguised as progress.

punchline.text: A blank check. With a prewritten loss.

quiz.question: Why were SPACs attractive to companies going public?
options: Less regulatory scrutiny and the ability to project future revenue

hook.text: In January 2021, a Reddit forum turned GameStop into a $80 billion company. Hedge funds lost $6 billion in days.

buildup.text: WallStreetBets identified heavily shorted stocks and coordinated mass buying. A short squeeze sent prices vertical.

discovery.text: Social media replaced institutional research. Memes became investment theses. Irony became market strategy.

twist.text: Robinhood halted buying, protecting hedge funds. Retail investors felt the system was rigged against them.

climax.text: Meme stocks showed retail power but also its limits. Most holders who bought the top lost money.

punchline.text: The internet beat Wall Street. Briefly.

quiz.question: What made GameStop's stock surge in January 2021?
options: A coordinated short squeeze by retail investors

hook.text: WeWork filed to IPO at $47 billion in 2019. The prospectus revealed billions in losses and the plan collapsed.

buildup.text: In hot markets, companies rush to go public. IPO windows open when investors are euphoric and prices are forgiving.

discovery.text: First-day IPO pops benefit insiders and underwriters. Retail investors who buy at the open often overpay.

twist.text: Many 2021 IPOs are now 80% below their listing price. The IPO window slammed shut in 2022 as rates rose.

climax.text: IPO frenzy is a bubble indicator. When unproven companies go public easily, euphoria has replaced scrutiny.

punchline.text: The best time to IPO is the worst time to buy.

quiz.question: Why is a surge in IPOs considered a bubble indicator?
options: It means the economy is healthy
Euphoria has replaced scrutiny for unproven companies

hook.text: Las Vegas home prices rose 134% between 2000 and 2006. Then they fell 62%. Entire neighborhoods were abandoned.

buildup.text: Easy credit, liar loans, and speculation turned houses into lottery tickets. Flippers bought and resold homes fast.

discovery.text: Banks stopped checking if borrowers could pay. No income? No problem. The loan was approved anyway.

twist.text: When prices fell, underwater homeowners walked away. Banks held homes they couldn't sell. The financial system froze.

climax.text: The housing crash caused the worst recession since the 1930s. Eight million jobs lost. A generation scarred.

punchline.text: Houses are shelter. They became casino chips.

quiz.question: What were 'liar loans'?

hook.text: Ordos, China, was built for 1 million people. In 2013, barely 100,000 lived there. Skyscrapers stood empty.

buildup.text: China's growth model relied on construction. Build first, find residents later. GDP targets drove building.

discovery.text: Real estate represented 30% of China's GDP. Citizens invested lifetime savings into apartments as wealth storage.

twist.text: Evergrande, China's largest developer, defaulted on $300 billion in debt in 2021. The bubble began to crack.

climax.text: Millions of pre-sold apartments were never finished. Buyers paying mortgages on homes that don't exist.

punchline.text: Build it and they'll come. Unless they don't.

quiz.question: What happened with Evergrande in 2021?
options: It became the world's largest company
It defaulted on $300 billion in debt
It merged with a state-owned company

hook.text: Spain built more houses between 2000 and 2007 than France, Germany, and UK combined. Most were unneeded.

buildup.text: Euro adoption gave Spain and Ireland access to cheap German interest rates. Borrowing exploded.

discovery.text: Construction became Spain's main employer. Ireland's banks lent recklessly. Both economies were hostage to housing.

twist.text: Ireland's bank bailout cost 42% of GDP. Spain's unemployment hit 27%. Youth unemployment exceeded 50%.

climax.text: Joining the euro removed interest rate protection. Countries couldn't adjust monetary policy to local conditions.

punchline.text: Cheap money built too much. Expensive reality followed.

quiz.question: Why did Spain and Ireland experience such severe housing bubbles?
options: Cheap euro-denominated credit fueled excessive building

hook.text: The average home in Toronto costs $1.1 million. The average household income is $84,000. The math doesn't work.

buildup.text: Canada's housing prices rose 300% since 2000, driven by low rates, immigration, and limited supply.

discovery.text: Canadian household debt is 180% of income—highest in the G7. Much of it is mortgage debt.

twist.text: When the Bank of Canada raised rates in 2022, variable-rate mortgage holders saw payments jump 40% overnight.

climax.text: Whether Canada experiences a crash or a slow correction, an entire generation is priced out of ownership.

punchline.text: A house shouldn't take a lifetime to afford.

quiz.question: What makes Canada's housing market fragile?
options: Household debt at 180% of income, mostly mortgages

hook.text: Dubai built the world's tallest building during a real estate boom. Three months after completion, prices had halved.

buildup.text: Dubai transformed from a fishing village to a global hub in 20 years, fueled by oil money and speculation.

discovery.text: Foreign investors bought off-plan properties, flipping contracts before buildings were finished.

twist.text: In 2009, Dubai World asked to delay $26 billion in debt payments. The city-state nearly defaulted.

climax.text: Abu Dhabi bailed Dubai out with $10 billion. The skyline survived, but the lesson about speculation didn't stick.

punchline.text: Build the future. On borrowed money.

quiz.question: What happened to Dubai real estate prices after the Burj Khalifa was completed?

buildup.text: Bitcoin started as a peer-to-peer payment experiment. It became digital gold, then a speculative asset.

discovery.text: Bitcoin has no earnings, no dividends, no cash flow. Its value is whatever the next buyer will pay.

twist.text: Each crash was called the death of Bitcoin. Each recovery proved skeptics wrong—until the next crash.

climax.text: Is Bitcoin a bubble or a new asset class? After 15 years, the debate is as alive as the price volatility.

punchline.text: Either it's the future. Or the biggest bubble ever.

quiz.question: What makes Bitcoin difficult to value?
options: It has no earnings, dividends, or cash flow
It's controlled by a single company

hook.text: In 2017, a company raised $150 million in an ICO with a whitepaper and no product. It disappeared with the money.

buildup.text: Initial coin offerings let anyone create a token and sell it. Over $20 billion was raised in 2017-2018.

discovery.text: ICOs bypassed securities laws. No audits, no regulations, no investor protections. Buyer beware, literally.

twist.text: Eighty percent of ICOs were scams or failed projects. The SEC eventually declared most were illegal securities.

climax.text: The ICO craze mirrored the dot-com boom: revolutionary technology, zero due diligence, catastrophic losses.

punchline.text: A whitepaper is not a business plan.

quiz.question: What percentage of ICOs were scams or failed projects?

hook.text: In March 2021, a digital image by Beeple sold for $69 million at Christie's. It was a JPEG.

buildup.text: NFTs—non-fungible tokens—proved ownership of digital items on the blockchain. Art, music, tweets became collectibles.

discovery.text: NFT trading volume hit $25 billion in 2021. Celebrities, brands, and amateurs all created and sold digital art.

twist.text: By 2023, 95% of NFTs were worth nothing. The JPEG you bought for $10,000 couldn't sell for $10.

climax.text: NFTs had real use cases—tickets, identity, contracts—but speculation drowned them in hype and fraud.

punchline.text: Right-click. Save as. Move on.

quiz.question: What happened to 95% of NFTs by 2023?

hook.text: In May 2022, $60 billion vanished in 72 hours. Terra's stablecoin lost its peg and Luna went to zero.

buildup.text: Terra offered 20% yields on deposits. Investors deposited billions, drawn by returns no bank could match.

discovery.text: The system was algorithmic—no real assets backed the stablecoin. Trust in the algorithm was the only collateral.

twist.text: When confidence broke, the algorithm couldn't stabilize. It entered a death spiral: selling created more selling.

climax.text: The founder was later arrested. But the real lesson is that unsustainable yields always end the same way.

punchline.text: Twenty percent returns. Zero percent chance it lasts.

quiz.question: What backed Terra's stablecoin?
options: An algorithm with no real assets

hook.text: Nvidia's stock rose 800% in 18 months after ChatGPT launched. The AI chip company is worth $3 trillion.

buildup.text: AI is genuinely transformative. But so were railways, the internet, and crypto. Each spawned a bubble.

discovery.text: Real technology + excessive speculation = bubble. The technology being real doesn't prevent overvaluation.

twist.text: Most AI startups burn cash with no clear path to profit. Sound familiar? It should. 1999 called.

climax.text: AI will change the world. The question is whether current valuations already price in decades of future growth.

punchline.text: The tech is real. The prices might not be.

quiz.question: Why might AI be in a bubble despite being real technology?
options: Current prices may already reflect decades of future growth

hook.text: Glass-Steagall separated banks from casinos in 1933. It was repealed in 1999. The 2008 crash followed nine years later.

buildup.text: After every crash, new rules are written: SEC after 1929, Dodd-Frank after 2008, crypto regulations after 2022.

discovery.text: Regulations work—for a while. They prevent the exact same crisis from happening again in the exact same way.

twist.text: But innovation creates new loopholes. Shadow banking, DeFi, and SPACs all exploited gaps in existing rules.

climax.text: The pattern: crash, regulate, forget, deregulate, innovate around rules, crash again. Memory fades every 20 years.

punchline.text: We regulate the last crisis. Never the next one.

quiz.question: Why do financial regulations eventually fail to prevent new crises?
options: Innovation creates new products that exploit gaps in existing rules

hook.text: Alan Greenspan saw the dot-com bubble forming in 1996. He called it 'irrational exuberance.' Then he did nothing.

buildup.text: Central banks face a dilemma: should they pop bubbles early or clean up after the crash?

discovery.text: Popping bubbles means raising rates, which hurts the whole economy. The cure might be worse than the disease.

twist.text: Greenspan chose to clean up after. He cut rates post-crash, which fueled the next bubble in housing.

climax.text: There's no good answer. Act early and you're the villain who killed growth. Act late and you failed to prevent disaster.

punchline.text: Pop it early or pick up the pieces. Both hurt.

quiz.question: What did Greenspan do after identifying 'irrational exuberance'?
options: Did nothing and planned to clean up after

hook.text: In 2008, banks gambled, lost, and got bailed out. In 2023, Silicon Valley Bank collapsed and was rescued too.

buildup.text: Moral hazard: if you know you'll be rescued, you take bigger risks. Bailouts create incentive to misbehave.

discovery.text: Too-big-to-fail means the biggest banks can gamble freely. Losses are socialized while profits stay private.

twist.text: Not bailing out Lehman caused a global crisis. So politicians learned: always bail out. Which is also a problem.

climax.text: The system rewards risky behavior and punishes caution. The careful bank earns less than the reckless one.

punchline.text: Heads I win. Tails you bail me out.

quiz.question: What is moral hazard in banking?
options: Taking bigger risks because you expect to be bailed out

hook.text: Only 33% of adults worldwide can answer three basic financial questions about interest, inflation, and risk.

buildup.text: Most bubble victims aren't greedy—they're uninformed. They buy because others buy, not because they understand.

discovery.text: Countries with mandatory financial education—Australia, Japan—have lower rates of consumer fraud and debt default.

twist.text: Financial education alone can't prevent bubbles. Even experts like Citigroup's CEO said you have to keep dancing.

climax.text: Literacy helps individuals but not systems. Bubbles are collective phenomena that override individual knowledge.

punchline.text: Know the math. Still feel the herd.

quiz.question: Can financial literacy alone prevent bubbles?
options: Yes, educated investors never lose money
No, bubbles are collective phenomena that override individual knowledge
Yes, but only in developed countries

hook.text: The dot-com bubble wasted billions but funded the fiber optic cables that power today's internet.

buildup.text: Economist Carlota Perez argues every technological revolution follows the same cycle: bubble, crash, deployment.

discovery.text: Bubbles overfund new technology. The excess capital builds infrastructure that wouldn't exist under rational investment.

twist.text: Railway mania, canal mania, electrification, the internet—each destroyed fortunes but left lasting infrastructure.

climax.text: Bubbles are painful but productive. The question isn't whether they happen—it's how to distribute the pain fairly.

punchline.text: Bubbles build the future. On other people's money.

quiz.question: According to Carlota Perez, what useful role do bubbles play?
options: They overfund technology, creating infrastructure that outlasts the crash
